observation: Running large language model (LLM) inference over large relational datasets for batch data analytics is extremely slow and expensive: an NVIDIA L4 GPU serving Llama3-8B processes only about 6 KB of text per second, taking roughly a day to handle 15 GB of data, and processing a comparable amount of data on OpenAI's GPT-4o costs about $10K. Although LLM invocations are increasingly offered as operators on relational tables, naively sending rows in their default order to a serving backend with a prompt KV cache leads to low cache-hit rates. Real relational workloads contain repeated cell values, joined-feature repetition, popular-item reuse, and shared RAG contexts that could serve as cached prefixes; but tables also contain highly unique leading fields such as IDs or review text, and the fixed row/field order in which requests are sent critically limits how much prefix reuse is possible.

claims: LLMs are autoregressive Transformer models that generate text token by token and can store computed attention states as key-value (KV) cache.

LLM inference engines typically batch requests continuously to improve throughput, but KV-cache memory can be very large: up to 800KB per token for a 13B model and up to 1.6GB for a typical 2,000-token request.
Recent work leverages prompt caching by storing attention states of frequently reused prompt segments in KV cache and reusing shared prefixes to reduce inference latency.
Cached-prompt reuse is now offered as a service by model providers at a fraction of the price of uncached prompts.

claims: Several systems and APIs support calling LLMs as operators over relational data, and LOTUS is an example programming framework that enables semantic queries with LLMs over tables of unstructured and structured data.
These LLM-over-tables systems provide SQL/DataFrame-style integration, but they do not explore reordering table rows and fields to optimize KV-cache hits.

claims: Real-world relational databases exhibit repetitive data patterns, and columnar storage systems exploit repeated values across fields for compression while related techniques such as run-length encoding, multi-relational data mining, and correlation analysis use data relationships to optimize query execution.

Relational queries create data groupings based on access patterns, and techniques such as database cracking, multidimensional clustering, and Delta Lake Z-order reorganize data according to query patterns.

solution.idea: The observation sits at a mismatch between how LLM serving systems reuse prefixes and how relational operators present prompts. vLLM, SGLang, Prompt Cache, and Hydragen all cache exact token prefixes, but they assume the caller supplies prompts in an order and with an internal column order that exposes reusable prefixes. LOTUS already exposes LLM invocations as relational operators over tables, but it runs prompts in the table's default row/field order; it does not choose a row or field order for KV-cache hits. Data-management techniques such as C-store's column organization, CORDS-style correlation discovery, database cracking, and Delta Lake Z-order reorganize for compression or tuple access locality, not for token-prefix reuse. Consequently, in a default row a highly unique leading field such as a primary key or review text causes every prompt to diverge immediately after the shared instruction. Any repeated dimension, join feature, popular item, or RAG context that appears later is useless to a prefix cache because all later tokens occur after an already-unique prefix. The core idea is therefore to introduce an explicit prompt-layout and request-scheduling layer between a relational LLM operator and the serving backend. The layer treats each row as a sequence of labeled field segments and chooses, for a given table and operator, (1) a field order inside the prompt and (2) a row emission order. Repeated and long shared values, correlated attributes, and RAG contexts should be moved to the left of unique values because KV-cache reuse is prefix-based: only a token sequence that appears at the beginning of many rows can be amortized. Row order should be a depth-first traversal of the trie of common prefixes, ordered by prefix popularity, so the cache serves one group before another and does not evict a large common prefix before all of its rows have been processed. This gives the serving backends the exact stream their mechanisms already expect: rows sharing long prefixes arrive contiguously, and the expensive first token of each prompt is not recomputed for every row. The direction deliberately does not modify the attention model, inference engine, or relational semantics; it only changes the order of tokens and rows that the operator presents, which is a legal and transparent optimization when the prompt is generated from structured, labeled table rows. The main design trade-off is that reordering fields changes the literal prompt and can, in principle, change an LLM's output; the solution handles this by applying layout planning only to safe structured serializations or to contexts that are semantically order-insensitive, and by treating row permutation as harmless because per-row LLM calls are independent. Another trade-off is sorting overhead: a full row sort of a large table is expensive, so possible savings have to exceed the sort cost, and the layout should be used repeatedly or amortized through cracking-style adaptive reordering. Alternatives considered and rejected include relying on the serving engine's scheduler alone, because it cannot discover prefixes the caller never exposes; grouping rows by an existing low-cardinality column alone, because if the manifest order still begins with unique IDs the shared field never becomes a prefix; batching many rows into one prompt, which changes the operator contract and does not generalize; and exhaustive search over all field permutations and row orders, which would be far too costly. The chosen approach is a greedy, statistics-driven construction of a prefix trie, justified by the structure of the problem: prefix reuse is a hierarchical property, and at each level the field that creates the most shared token mass should be placed next.
solution.implementation: The implementation is a four-module optimizer interposed between a Spark/LOTUS-style relational plan and a vLLM/SGLang-style serving endpoint. Module 1, operator capture and safety classification, identifies every place in an incoming query plan where an LLM is invoked per table row. For each such operator the optimizer receives the projected relation R, the prompt template, and the list of fields used to construct the prompt. If a template is free-form natural language whose meaning depends on exact field order, the optimizer marks it unsafe and does not rewrite it; for a typical relational LLM operator that materializes each row as a labeled structure such as f1=v1; f2=v2; ..., the optimizer classifies the operation as safe and stores the canonical serialization function. Row permutation is always safe because each row is an independent inference call. Module 2, profiler, takes a bounded random sample S of R. For every field f in the prompt it records the distinct values and their observed frequencies, and it estimates the token cost of serializing each value, including field name, delimiter, and the value text. If an open tokenizer is available, the cost is obtained by tokenizing the sampled serialized value; otherwise a character-length proxy is used. The profiler additionally computes lightweight CORDS-style correlations among fields so that the planner can recognize when one field almost functionally determines another; these correlations are used to push correlated repeated fields together and to avoid considering obviously redundant candidates. Module 3, prefix layout planner, greedily constructs an ordered field list. It maintains a collection of live prefix groups. Initially there is one live group containing all sampled rows, representing the common static instruction and any system/RAG prefix. At each step it considers every unassigned field f. For each live group G and each distinct value v of f inside G, let n(G,v) be the number of sampled rows in G whose value of f is v, and let len(G,v) be the estimated token length of serialized substring for f=v. The candidate score is score(f) = sum over live groups G, sum over distinct values v of max(0, n(G,v)-1) * len(G,v). This score is the amount of token mass that would be shared only if f is placed at the current prefix position. A unique-valued field has score zero because no sampled rows share it. A constant field, a low-cardinality popular dimension, or a long repeated RAG context receives a high score. The planner appends the field with maximum score to the ordered prefix list. It then splits every live group by the values of the selected field; groups with fewer than tau_min sampled rows are removed from live consideration, tau_min being a configuration parameter defaulting to a small multiple of the serving engine's cache block size. If the number of live groups exceeds G_max, splitting stops. If no remaining field has positive score, or all fields are assigned, the loop ends. All remaining fields are appended after the chosen prefix fields in their original schema order. The output of Module 3 is a KV-friendly layout: a prefix column order of length k, followed by the rest. The key property is that rows sharing a full prefix of the first k fields also share a long token prefix in their constructed prompts, while unique fields appear only after the prefix has already been rebuilt by the cache. Module 4, materializer and request streamer, applies the layout to the full relation. It reorders the projection so that each row is serialized in the planned field order. To obtain the row stream order, it computes, for every prefix level j from 1 to k, the relation C_j = group by the first j ordered fields and count rows. Let cnt_j be that count for a row's prefix value. The module performs an exchange and sort on the composite key (descending cnt_1, ascending value_o1, descending cnt_2, ascending value_o2, ..., descending cnt_k, ascending value_ok). Sorting first by group counts, then by the serialized prefix value, visits sibling prefix groups in decreasing popularity while keeping every group contiguous. This is a depth-first traversal of the prefix trie ordered by group size, so a large shared context is presented while it is still cached, and the backend's radix or paged KV cache automatically finds the reusable prefix from the previously sent group. The request streamer consumes rows in this order and constructs each prompt as the static instruction followed by the ordered labeled fields and then any remaining original fields. Prompts are sent continuously to the serving endpoint in batches compatible with the backend's maximum sequence length. Because the prompts within a batch and across consecutive batches share prefixes, the cache does useful work; the solution does not need to change vLLM/SGLang. For repeated or recurring analytic workloads, the materialized sorted view can be persisted as a Delta Lake table clustered by the same ordered prefix columns, using Z-order or sorted layout, so later invocations of the same LLM operator do not pay the sort cost again; when access patterns change, database-cracking-style adaptive repartitioning is used to reorder only the affected prefix ranges. All configurable parameters are exposed: tau_min, the minimum number of rows in a prefix group that justifies further splitting; G_max, a cap on live groups to bound planner and sorting memory; and the choice of whether a prompt template is in the safe structured class. The implementation contains no new inference logic and no change to the Transformer's attention computation; it only exposes the cacheable prefix structure that is already latent in the relational values and addresses the observation's root cause directly.
